title: Three Units of Digit Weight
statement: How many positive integers less than $10^{25}$ have decimal digits that sum to $3$ and are divisible by $37$?
hints: A number whose digits sum to $3$ can be built by adding three powers of $10$, possibly with repeats. Write it this way and consider which exponents are allowed.
Work modulo $37$. Since $999 = 27 \cdot 37$, we have $10^3 \equiv 1 \pmod{37}$, so the residue of a power of $10$ depends only on its exponent modulo $3$.

The powers of $10$ have residues $1$, $10$ and $26$ modulo $37$. Writing the number as a sum of three powers of $10$, test all the ways of adding three of these residues. The only sum that is a multiple of $37$ is $1 + 10 + 26$, so the three exponents must lie in different classes modulo $3$. It remains to count the exponents from $0$ to $24$ in each class and combine these counts.
solution: A positive integer less than $10^{25}$ with digit sum $3$ has the form $n = 10^a + 10^b + 10^c$ with $0 \le a \le b \le c \le 24$. Conversely, every such sum has digit sum $3$ and is less than $10^{25}$, because no carrying occurs and the sum has at most $25$ digits. The digit in position $k$ of $n$ equals the number of times $k$ appears among $a, b, c$, so each integer corresponds to exactly one multiset of exponents. Since $999 = 27 \cdot 37$, we have $10^3 \equiv 1 \pmod{37}$. Hence $10^k$ is congruent to $1$, $10$ or $26$ modulo $37$ when $k \equiv 0$, $1$ or $2 \pmod 3$ respectively, where $26 \equiv 100 \pmod{37}$. The ten possible sums of three of these residues are $$1+1+1=3,\quad 1+1+10=12,\quad 1+1+26=28,\quad 1+10+10=21,\quad 1+10+26=37,$$ $$1+26+26=53,\quad 10+10+10=30,\quad 10+10+26=46,\quad 10+26+26=62,\quad 26+26+26=78.$$ The only multiple of $37$ in this list is $37 = 1 + 10 + 26$. So $37 \mid n$ exactly when $a, b, c$ lie in three different classes modulo $3$. In particular, the exponents are distinct, so the digits $2$ and $3$ cannot occur. Among $0, 1, \dots, 24$, the class of $0$ modulo $3$ contains $9$ exponents ($0, 3, \dots, 24$), the class of $1$ contains $8$ ($1, 4, \dots, 22$), and the class of $2$ contains $8$ ($2, 5, \dots, 23$). Choosing one exponent from each class gives a unique set of three exponents, and hence a unique integer $n$. Every valid $n$ arises in this way. The number of such integers is therefore $9 \cdot 8 \cdot 8 = 576$. The answer is $576$. Why this works. modular-arithmetic, rule-of-product: the powers of $10$ take only three residues modulo $37$, which turns divisibility into independent choices of one exponent from each class.
